title: Machine Learning, from Models to MLOps
description: Fit, evaluate and ship machine-learning models: loss and gradient descent, honest metrics, generalisation, trees and networks, then pipelines, serving and drift monitoring.
audience: A capable adult who can write Python and read basic statistics. No prior machine learning is assumed. Plan to take this before ai-engineering, which uses precision, recall and the idea of a held-out set.
outcomes: You'll be able to fit a simple model by hand and read its error.
You'll be able to take gradient descent steps and tune a learning rate.
You'll be able to compute precision, recall, F1 and AUC and choose among them.
You'll be able to diagnose overfitting and prevent leakage.
You'll be able to describe how to reproduce, serve, monitor and govern a model.

modules.title: Learning from data
modules.summary: A model is a function fitted to examples; loss, gradient descent and honest metrics are the three tools that everything else builds on.

modules.title: Models that generalise
modules.summary: Why a model that fits its training data can still fail, and the methods that keep it honest: splits, regularisation, good features, trees and networks.

modules.title: From notebook to production
modules.summary: The work after the model: reproducible pipelines, serving, monitoring drift, and governing a model that real people depend on.

lessons.title: What a model learns from examples
lessons.objective: Fit a straight line to four points by least squares and read the result as a model with parameters, predictions and errors.

concepts.title: Model
concepts.summary: A function with adjustable parameters that maps features to a prediction.

concepts.title: Parameters
concepts.summary: The numbers a learning procedure adjusts so that predictions match the training examples.

concepts.title: Residual
concepts.summary: The difference between an observed label and the model's prediction for it.

misconceptions: Learners often think the model stores the examples; a fitted line keeps only two numbers and discards the data.
A good fit is often read as a true law, when it only describes this sample.
sequence: Four examples (hours studied, score) as points on a plane.
A rule ŷ = w·x + b, with w and b free.
Choosing the parameters that make squared residuals smallest, with the closed form w = Sxy/Sxx and b = ȳ − w·x̄.
Predict for a new input and compute the error on the examples.
examples: Residuals 0.1, 0.2, −0.7, 0.4; squares sum to 0.70; MSE = 0.175.

figures.shows: The four points with an adjustable line and vertical residual segments, using a different dataset from the question so the fitted slope is not shown.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the slope and watch the sum of squared residuals change on the demonstration data.

figures.shows: A blank residual table for the learner to fill after the worked example; no filled values before the question.
figures.learnerAction: none

questionPlan.sample: For the points (1,2), (2,4), (3,5), (4,8) the least-squares line is y = w·x. What is w?

historyNotes: Legendre published least squares in 1805 and Gauss claimed earlier use, in his 1809 work on planetary orbits.

lessons.title: Loss and gradient descent
lessons.objective: Take gradient descent steps by hand on a one-parameter model and explain how the learning rate changes the result.

concepts.title: Loss function
concepts.summary: A single number that scores how wrong the model's predictions are on the data.

concepts.title: Gradient
concepts.summary: The slope of the loss with respect to a parameter, which points towards increasing loss.

concepts.title: Learning rate
concepts.summary: The step size multiplier applied to the gradient on each update.

misconceptions: The gradient points to the minimum; it points uphill, so the update subtracts it.
A larger learning rate always trains faster; past a threshold the loss grows.
sequence: Why closed-form solutions stop working for large models.
The model ŷ = w·x and loss L(w) = ½·Σ(w·xᵢ − yᵢ)² on points (1,2),(2,4).
The gradient dL/dw = Σ xᵢ(w·xᵢ − yᵢ) and the update w ← w − η·gradient.
Too small, about right and too large step sizes.
examples: At w = 0: L = (4+16)/2 = 10, gradient = 1·(−2)+2·(−4) = −10; with η = 0.1, w becomes 1.0 and L falls to 2.5.
Next step: gradient −5, w = 1.5, L = 0.625. With η = 1.0 from w = 0, w jumps to 10 and L rises to 160.

figures.shows: The loss curve L(w) as a parabola with the current w marked and the tangent drawn.
figures.learnerAction: Step once at a time and choose the learning rate; see the point walk down or bounce out.

figures.shows: Columns for w, gradient and loss, filled only for a demonstration dataset and left empty for the question's data.
figures.learnerAction: none

questionPlan.sample: Model ŷ = w·x, points (1,2),(2,4), loss ½Σ(w·x−y)². At w = 0 the gradient is −10. With learning rate 0.1, what is w after one step?
Continue from w = 1. What is the gradient there?
From w = 0 you use learning rate 1.0 and the loss rises from 10 to 160. What went wrong?
questionPlan.answer: The step was so large that it overshot the minimum
choices: The step was so large that it overshot the minimum
The gradient had the wrong sign
The loss function is not differentiable

historyNotes: Augustin-Louis Cauchy described gradient descent in 1847; the stochastic version goes back to Robbins and Monro in 1951.

lessons.title: Classification and the confusion matrix
lessons.objective: Compute accuracy, precision, recall and F1 from a confusion matrix and say why accuracy misleads on imbalanced data.

concepts.title: Confusion matrix
concepts.summary: A table of true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives.

concepts.title: Precision and recall
concepts.summary: Precision is TP/(TP+FP) and recall is TP/(TP+FN).

concepts.title: Base rate
concepts.summary: The share of examples that belong to the positive class.

misconceptions: High accuracy means a good model; with 6% positives a model that always says negative scores 94%.
Precision and recall measure the same thing from two sides.
sequence: A spam or fraud filter on 1,000 messages.
The four cells and what each means for a user.
Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and which errors cost more.
A baseline that predicts the majority class.
examples: The all-negative baseline scores 940/1000 = 0.94 accuracy with recall 0.

figures.learnerAction: Click a cell to highlight which metric uses it.

figures.learnerAction: Toggle between model and always-negative baseline.

lessons.title: Thresholds, ROC and AUC
lessons.objective: Move a decision threshold, recompute precision and recall, and compute AUC as the fraction of correctly ordered positive-negative pairs.

concepts.title: Decision threshold
concepts.summary: The score above which a classifier predicts the positive class.

concepts.title: ROC curve
concepts.summary: True positive rate plotted against false positive rate across all thresholds.

concepts.title: AUC
concepts.summary: The probability that a random positive scores higher than a random negative.

misconceptions: A classifier has one precision and one recall; both change with the threshold.
An AUC of 0.9 means 90% accuracy.
sequence: Six scored examples, three positive.
A threshold turns scores into decisions and moves cases between cells.
Sweeping the threshold traces the ROC curve.
AUC counts correctly ordered pairs.
examples: Scores 0.9, 0.8, 0.6, 0.55, 0.4, 0.3 with labels 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0. Threshold 0.5: TP 3, FP 1, FN 0, precision 0.75, recall 1.0, FPR 1/3. Threshold 0.7: TP 2, FP 0, FN 1, precision 1.0, recall 2/3.
Positive-negative pairs: 9; ordered correctly: 8 (the 0.55 positive loses to the 0.6 negative), so AUC = 8/9 ≈ 0.889.

figures.shows: ROC curve with a movable point for the current threshold.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the threshold slider; the confusion counts and the ROC point update.

figures.shows: Sorted scores and labels with the pair-counting grid left blank until the learner has answered.
figures.learnerAction: none

questionPlan.sample: Scores 0.9, 0.8, 0.6, 0.55, 0.4, 0.3 have labels 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0. At threshold 0.5, what is the precision?

historyNotes: ROC analysis came from radar signal detection in the Second World War; Fawcett's 2006 tutorial is the standard machine-learning introduction.

lessons.title: Generalisation and the test set
lessons.objective: Split data into training, validation and test sets and diagnose overfitting from the gap between training and validation error.

concepts.title: Overfitting
concepts.summary: Fitting noise in the training set so that error on new data is much worse than error on training data.

concepts.title: Validation set
concepts.summary: Held-out data used to choose between models or settings.

concepts.title: Test set
concepts.summary: Held-out data used once, at the end, to estimate performance on new data.

misconceptions: Low training error shows the model is good.
Using the test set repeatedly while tuning is harmless; each look leaks a little information.
sequence: Polynomial fits of rising degree to 10 noisy points.
Training error falls with complexity while validation error falls and then rises.
Why three splits and what each is for.
Time-ordered data must be split by time.
examples: 1,000 rows split 70/15/15 gives 700 train, 150 validation, 150 test.
Training accuracy 0.99, validation accuracy 0.82: a gap of 0.17, overfitting. Training 0.84 and validation 0.82 with both low is underfitting if the target is 0.95.

lessons.title: Regularisation and cross-validation
lessons.objective: Add an L2 or L1 penalty to a loss, and average a metric over k folds to compare two models.

concepts.title: Regularisation
concepts.summary: Adding a penalty on parameter size to the loss so that the fit prefers simpler models.

concepts.title: Cross-validation
concepts.summary: Rotating which fold is held out so every example is used for validation once.

concepts.title: Bias and variance
concepts.summary: Bias is error from wrong assumptions; variance is sensitivity to the particular training sample.

misconceptions: Regularisation always improves accuracy; it trades training fit for stability.
Cross-validation gives a model; it gives an estimate for choosing among settings.
sequence: The penalised loss L(w) + λ·w² and what λ controls.
L1 penalises |w| and tends to zero out parameters.
Five-fold cross-validation, one fold held out at a time.
Comparing two settings by mean and spread across folds.
examples: Fold accuracies 0.82, 0.80, 0.85, 0.78, 0.80 average 0.81. On 1,000 rows five folds train on 800 and validate on 200.

lessons.title: Features, scaling and leakage
lessons.objective: Prepare features with scaling, encoding and imputation, and spot target leakage and preprocessing leakage.

concepts.title: Scaling
concepts.summary: Rescaling a numeric feature, for example to zero mean and unit variance or to the range 0 to 1.

concepts.title: One-hot encoding
concepts.summary: Replacing a category by one 0/1 column per level.

concepts.title: Leakage
concepts.summary: Information in training that will not exist at prediction time, or test information used in preparation.

misconceptions: Fitting the scaler on all the data before splitting is harmless.
A feature that predicts the label almost perfectly is a great find; it is usually a leak.
sequence: Features [10,20,30,40,50] standardised and min-max scaled.
Median against mean imputation for a skewed column.

lessons.title: Decision trees and ensembles
lessons.objective: Choose a split by Gini impurity and explain why a vote of many different trees beats one deep tree.

concepts.title: Gini impurity
concepts.summary: 1 minus the sum of squared class proportions in a node.

concepts.title: Bagging
concepts.summary: Training models on bootstrap resamples and combining their votes.

concepts.title: Random forest
concepts.summary: Bagged trees that also consider only a random subset of features at each split.

misconceptions: A deeper tree is always better; a full-depth tree memorises.
Averaging copies of the same model helps; the models must differ.
sequence: A node of 10 examples, 6 positive and 4 negative.
Gini impurity, a candidate split and the weighted child impurity.
Variance of a single deep tree; bootstrap resamples and voting.
Out-of-bag rows as a free validation set.
examples: Parent Gini = 1 − 0.36 − 0.16 = 0.48; left (4 pos, 1 neg) 0.32, right (2 pos, 3 neg) 0.48, weighted 0.40, gain 0.08.
Five trees vote 1,0,1,1,0 and the forest predicts 1. A row is missed by a 10-row bootstrap with probability 0.9¹⁰ ≈ 0.349.

lessons.title: Neural networks from one neuron up
lessons.objective: Run a forward pass through one neuron and count the parameters of a small fully connected network.

concepts.title: Neuron
concepts.summary: A weighted sum of inputs plus a bias, passed through an activation function.

concepts.title: Activation function
concepts.summary: A nonlinear function such as ReLU or sigmoid applied after the weighted sum.

concepts.title: Backpropagation
concepts.summary: Applying the chain rule backwards through a network to get the gradient of the loss for every parameter.

misconceptions: Stacking linear layers adds power; without a nonlinearity they collapse to one linear map.
Backpropagation is a different learning algorithm from gradient descent; it computes the gradients that descent uses.
sequence: One neuron with two inputs.
ReLU and sigmoid.
Layers in sequence and parameter counts.
The chain rule delivers each weight's gradient.
examples: A 4-3-2 network has (4·3+3) + (3·2+2) = 15 + 8 = 23 parameters.

lessons.title: Pipelines and experiment tracking
lessons.objective: Say what must be recorded to reproduce a training run and count the fits in a hyperparameter search.

concepts.title: Pipeline
concepts.summary: A fixed sequence of preparation and training steps run the same way every time.

concepts.title: Experiment tracking
concepts.summary: Recording code version, data version, parameters, seed and metrics for every run.

concepts.title: Reproducibility
concepts.summary: Getting the same result again from the same recorded inputs.

misconceptions: Saving the model file is enough; without the data version, nobody can say what it learned from.
Setting a random seed makes a run reproducible regardless of library or hardware.
sequence: Two notebook runs with different scores and no record of why.
What a run record contains.
Content hashes for data.
Grid search cost: configurations × folds.
examples: 3 learning rates × 4 depths × 5 folds = 60 fits.

lessons.title: Serving a model and releasing it safely
lessons.objective: Choose batch or online serving, size replicas for a latency target and describe a canary release.

concepts.title: Online serving
concepts.summary: Answering one request at a time within a latency budget.

concepts.title: Train-serve skew
concepts.summary: A difference between how features are computed in training and in production.

concepts.title: Canary release
concepts.summary: Sending a small share of traffic to a new model before a full rollout.

misconceptions: A model that passes offline evaluation is safe to ship; production data and feature code differ.
Rolling back a model is trivial; features and schemas may have changed with it.
sequence: Nightly scores versus per-request scores.
A 200 ms budget split across network, feature lookup and model.
Replica sizing from peak load and target utilisation.
Shadow, canary and rollback.
examples: Peak 400 requests/s, 50 requests/s per replica, 80% target utilisation: 400/(50·0.8) = 10 replicas.

lessons.title: Monitoring and drift
lessons.objective: Compute a population stability index and decide what to monitor when labels arrive late.

concepts.title: Data drift
concepts.summary: A change in the distribution of input features.

concepts.title: Concept drift
concepts.summary: A change in the relation between features and the label.

concepts.title: Population stability index
concepts.summary: Σ (actual% − expected%)·ln(actual%/expected%) across bins.

misconceptions: Stable accuracy means no drift; labels may be late, and input drift appears first.
A PSI threshold is a law; 0.1 and 0.25 are industry conventions.
sequence: A feature binned in training: 50/30/20 percent. This week: 40/30/30.
The PSI formula.
Data drift against concept drift against label delay.
Proxy metrics: input distributions, prediction distribution, business outcomes.

One fairness metric is the right one; several are mutually incompatible in general.
